result.summary:
Idiom/supervision/scope-creep review: (1) Idiomatic vs. crutch -- N/A for gen_statem (this is pure sandbox-construction, no state machine); Letflow.Engine.Lua.Sandbox is a plain data-driven module (a @sandbox_deny_set list of {path, reason} tuples consumed by new/1) which is the right shape for this problem -- no crutch pattern found. (2) Supervision -- N/A: sandbox.ex performs no process spawning, holds no state, and touches no instance/supervision tree; confirmed no file under lib/letflow/instance_supervisor.ex or process_instance.ex is touched by this diff (git diff --stat: only lib/letflow/engine/lua/sandbox.ex, mix.exs, mix.lock, test/letflow/engine/lua_script_audit_test.exs, plus design doc and prior handoffs). (3) Type-safety gaps -- none blocking; the deny_entry :: {[atom()], String.t()} shape is adequate for a fixed, compile-time-authored 28-entry list with no runtime construction of paths, so a struct/Ecto.Enum would add no unrepresentable-state protection here. Not filed as an issue. (4) Scope creep -- none found: new/1's opts parameter is unused today but exists specifically so REQ-152/154-156 can extend behavior without introducing a second Lua.new/1 call site (INV-SBX-1) -- this is forward-compatible API surface directly justified by decision 0014's own sequencing ('Lua lands first ... WASM ... conforms to it'), not framework machinery built ahead of need. Implementation matches the approved design faithfully: 28-entry deny-set with per-entry installed/vacuous reasoning verified against deps/lua source (not documentation), the coroutine non-entry decision with its stated reason, and the LUA-03 (three reasons)/LUA-04 (structural) moduledoc restatements match design §7/§8 in substance. Verified independently: mix compile --warnings-as-errors exits 0 with zero warnings; mix format --check-formatted exits 0 for all three changed files; mix test test/letflow/engine/lua_script_audit_test.exs -> 'Result: 16 passed', 0 failures; grep -rn "Lua\.new(" lib --include=*.ex returns exactly one hit (lib/letflow/engine/lua/sandbox.ex:206), confirming AC1/INV-SBX-1's single-call-site claim independently of SECURITY-REVIEWER's prior run of the same check. No entry in docs/anti-patterns.md applies to this diff (checked in full; no shared-state/singleton-process, no fragment/1 duplication, no timestamp-batching pattern present here).

AC5 RETIREMENT SIGN-OFF (explicit, reasoned, not a rubber-stamp): PASS -- consistent with both decision 0014 and REQ-058's own intent. REQ-058's AC5 read in full: 'mix.exs gains no Lua/NIF dependency, and the moduledoc states that the Lua execution runtime is S5 scope PENDING stage-5-scripting-plugins.md's build-vs-bind decision record' (docs/requirements.yaml REQ-058 entry, read directly). Three points settle this: (a) the acceptance criterion's own text is conditioned on the decision record being PENDING -- decision 0014 was decided 2026-08-23, so the literal precondition the AC was written against no longer holds; retiring a test whose premise has been overtaken by a since-settled decision record is not overriding REQ-058, it is recognizing REQ-058's own stated condition has resolved. (b) REQ-058's description text states the guard's purpose explicitly: 'Do NOT add a Lua dependency to mix.exs in THIS REQUIREMENT, and do NOT pre-empt S5's build-vs-bind decision by implicitly choosing a runtime' -- the guard's purpose was to stop REQ-058 (S3-stage, an audit-persistence path with an injected Executor interface) from silently picking a runtime ahead of the decision. It was never framed as a permanent prohibition on any future requirement ever adding the dependency; the dependency is now being added by REQ-151, which is S5-stage work executing decision 0014 itself, not S3-stage work pre-empting it. (c) decision 0014 explicitly assigns this exact sign-off to REVIEWER: 'REVIEWER owns sign-off on the first requirement that adds tv-labs/lua to mix.exs' -- this is precisely that occasion, and the decision record is the authority the original AC5 test was proxying for. The rewritten test (test/letflow/engine/lua_script_audit_test.exs:415-436) was VERIFIED to preserve regression coverage rather than delete it: it now asserts the {:lua, "~> 1.0"} dependency IS present (with an inline comment explaining why the original assertion's purpose no longer applies), so an accidental future removal of the dependency -- which would break sandbox.ex's compile -- is still caught. This satisfies this project's anti-pattern discipline against silently narrowing test coverage to make a gate pass.

ONE FLAG, non-blocking, filed as a follow-up rather than a FAIL condition: lib/letflow/engine/lua_script_audit.ex's own moduledoc (lines 16-21, untouched by this diff, correctly out of REQ-151's owned_modules per ELIXIR-DEV's explicit scope note) still reads 'S5's own build-vs-bind decision record ... is a prerequisite for whoever supplies a real Executor implementation' and the nested Executor.script_ref typedoc (lines 91-97) still says 'S5's build-vs-bind decision ... has not been made'. Both statements are now factually stale -- decision 0014 was decided 2026-08-23 and REQ-151 is already consuming it. This is a real documentation-consistency gap but does NOT block this PASS: (i) ELIXIR-DEV was explicitly instructed not to rewrite that moduledoc beyond what the remaining guardrail tests require, and the remaining tests ('the moduledoc states the Lua runtime is S5 scope, pending the build-vs-bind decision record' / checks for 'S5' and 'stage-5-scripting-plugins.md' substrings only) still pass truthfully against the unchanged text; (ii) REQ-058's own module is out of REQ-151's scope by design; (iii) no test or downstream consumer is misled by the staleness -- script_ref remains correctly opaque regardless of whether the decision record is 'pending' or 'decided', since REQ-153 (the Executor implementation) is what will actually resolve the type, not this comment. Recommend a small documentation-only follow-up (owned by ELIXIR-DEV or DOC-UPDATER, not scoped to REQ-151) to update lua_script_audit.ex's moduledoc/typedoc to say the decision is DECIDED (0014, 2026-08-23) and name REQ-151/REQ-153 as the requirements executing it, rather than leaving 'has not been made' / 'is a prerequisite' language live past the point where it stopped being true.
